en: In the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, the *Fo shuo Shenri jing* (The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Shenri) is not attributed to Dharmarakṣa; it is likely that Zhi Qian erroneously ascribed it to him.
It was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling at Mount Ling’uiding in the city of Rājagṛha, together with the Great [Saṃgha].
"I have one thousand two hundred and fifty followers.

At that time, there was a great and wealthy elder in the city of Rājagṛha named Cāla; his wealth and treasures were immeasurable, and he revered and believed in the Buddha-dharma, making offerings to the Saṅgha with a diligence that was difficult to equal.

The elder had a younger brother named Shenri (Sunakṣatra), who did not believe in the Buddha-dharma but followed various heterodox arts; seeing his elder brother revere the True Dharma, he constantly harbored resentment and jealousy. The teacher he served was named Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and his five hundred followers said to Shenri:
"Now your elder brother alone does not serve me; he does not know the true Way, yet instead believes in the Buddha."
At that time, Cāṇūra, having learned of the discussion shared by the followers of other paths, said to Śūnya:
"I wish to invite your teacher tomorrow; would you be willing to deign to visit my home?"
Śunika replied, "I shall go and inform him.
Śunika then went to his teacher's place, knelt down for a long time, and said:
"My elder brother now wishes to subdue and invite the great personages; he requests that you deign to visit his home for a meal tomorrow.
The Master said, "Very well!"
He immediately accepted the invitation.
Then Shenri returned and said to his elder brother, "I have now accepted the invitation; I shall come tomorrow."

At that time, Cāṇūra dispatched a messenger who dug a large pit five feet deep in the ground at the entrance; he filled the pit with blue mud and covered it thinly so that it appeared level with the surrounding ground.

Furthermore, he had prepared in advance five hundred footstools, each provided with only one leg and draped with cloth. He also prepared five hundred bowls of matured milk curds, using these offerings to await the heterodox practitioners.

When the appointed time arrived the following day, they went to the place of invitation. Those Nirgranthas lacked any sense of decorum; they entered the hall in disorder, crowding shoulder-to-shoulder and pushing forward. Upon reaching the gateway, they all caused one another to stumble and run, falling back into muddy pits and soiling their robes. Filled with indignation, they all desired to turn back and depart.
At that time, Cāṇūra sent someone to detain him and explain his intention, saying:
"This is an old mud pit; the practitioner did not know it and fell into this pit, but he did not do so intentionally. I hope you will not be angry, and I pray that you will come forward to eat."
They traded their robes and were all invited to enter.

As they passed through the doorway, a vessel of curd was first placed before each of them; having taken it in hand, he told them to sit down. Just as they sat upon the couches, the couches all overturned, causing the five hundred practitioners to fall prostrate to the ground. Those who held bowls of curd and gruel splashed and drenched their faces and their robes.
At that time, the various practitioners grew even more filled with resentment and said to Shenri:
"Now you have joined us and conspired with our elder brother to bring disgrace upon us; this is no small matter."
At that time, Shenri was also deeply distressed, as the practitioners, filled with anger, all abandoned him and departed.
Then, Jñāradatta again pulled him back and detained him, speaking to him with words of expedient means and parables:
"When you and your companions fell into the mud, your bodies were pitch black and extremely hideous, just like your current state."
"Now this curd is perfectly white, its color fresh and pure, just like the Way of the Buddha; you may likewise abandon the arts you practice and come to follow my Dharma.
The followers of other paths did not speak with him further, but departed in resentment.
On the day of Shen the following day, he went to the teacher’s abode, knelt for a long time, and said:
"My elder brother acted improperly and committed what was not in accordance with the Dharma; I truly did not know of it. I pray that you, Master, will show me compassion and do not reproach me."
"Even so, today we must repay our teacher for his grudge from yesterday.
My elder brother merely insulted you and your disciples with a mud pit and buttermilk; what I shall now repay you for will exceed that."

"Now, I shall invite the teacher whom my elder brother serves; I will have the ground inside the gate dug five *zhang* deep, place fire within it, and cover it over thinly. I will prepare various foods and drinks, all of which I shall mix with poison."
"When the Buddha comes here, if he does not fall into the fire pit, we shall distribute this poisoned rice and kill him with it; what do you think of this plan, Master?"
The teacher replied:

"As for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who possesses vast wisdom, is holy and majestic, and perceives the events of the past and future, he immediately knows in advance whatever others discuss; though you may wish to do so, I fear it cannot be accomplished."
Shenri spoke again: "I should first invite him;
if he accepts, it will mean he is ignorant; but if he is truly a wise sage, he will not accept my invitation."
The Master said, "Excellent!

At that time, Śreṇika left the city of Rājagṛha and went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. Arriving before the Buddha, he joined his palms in salutation and, after yielding in courtesy, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to invite the Buddha and his disciples; I pray that you would deign to visit my home for a modest meal.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
Thereupon, Shenri rejoiced and withdrew, returning to report to his teacher:
"The Buddha has accepted the invitation as if he were ignorant; we need only dig a pit and prepare poisoned rice."
At that time, all the various non-Buddhist practitioners were greatly elated, and as they passed the news from one to another, they considered it a great celebration.

Śoṇaka had a son named Candraprabha Kumāra (in the language of Han, "Moonlight"), who in his past lives had studied the Buddhist scriptures and the Way. Possessing a spirit of fierce resolve and setting his mind upon the Mahāyāna, he said to his father:

"The Buddha is a Great Sage whose supernatural powers have reached perfection; he knows the infinite past and perceives the boundless future. Even the thoughts and intentions of the wriggling and crawling insects, he knows them all in advance."
"Do not heed the words of these wicked and deluded people, lest you incur heavy retribution.
Then, Jñānadhvaja again addressed his father, saying:

"Even if the kalpa were to end and its fires filled the entirety of the three thousandfold world system, and even if one were to take all manner of poisons and heap them up like Mount Sumeru, they still could not move a single hair of the Buddha; how much less could this small pit possibly harm him?"

Now, what your father has done is like a firefly attempting to obscure the sun and moon with its own meager light; it is like a small bird wishing to crash through the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) with its body—it only succeeds in shattering itself, accomplishing nothing at all.
"Now, since the practitioners of other paths have prepared such things, there is no need to invite the Buddha.
Because his father did not believe him, he continued with his previous plot; when the time arrived the following day, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The offerings are already prepared; we pray that you will deign to come."
Thereupon, the Tathāgata rose and turned toward the path, emitting a great radiance that penetrated all things with clarity.

At that time, there were ten bodhisattvas from the ten directions, all of whom were *avaivartika* (non-regressive). Each bodhisattva arrived together with hundreds of millions of nayutas of countless bodhisattvas; they each brought precious flowers and famous sandalwood incense, and offered various musical performances to the World-Honored One. They proceeded to the city of Rājagṛha, desiring to behold the Tathāgata and be moved by his spiritual power.
At that time, the house of Shenri was filled with a golden light as brilliant as the sun.

Jianluofa said, "Now the Buddha has manifested a golden light within this house; because the Buddha is advancing toward the Way, such a response has occurred. We should go and stop him; we must not let him proceed."
The father still did not believe him.

At that time, Śunika’s first wife, named Yueyu (Candrāvatī), who was the mother of Caṇḍarava, beheld these miraculous omens and leaped for joy; she immediately resolved her mind upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Thereupon, Cāṇūra Dharma addressed his mother, saying:
"I shall now command the five hundred ladies-in-waiting to all adorn themselves and come forth to see the Tathāgata. Why is this?..."
"A World-Honored One is difficult to encounter; only once in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas does a Buddha appear.
The five hundred ladies all accepted this instruction and joyfully attended upon the Buddha.

When the Buddha entered the city and his feet stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the three thousandfold world-system shook violently. All those with illnesses were completely healed; the blind saw, the deaf heard, the mute and the crippled could speak, the lame walked, and the poison of those who had been poisoned ceased to take effect.

All musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; gold, silver, and the seven treasures all produced sounds; and birds and beasts flew and ran together, crying out in mournful harmony.
At that time, the deities of the ten directions, along with the various devas and humans, each accompanied by incalculable numbers of honored spirits, all followed him to the house of Shenri.

The Buddha stepped upon a fire pit, which was transformed into a bathing pool. Within it grew lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels, each with a thousand petals and stems made of the seven precious jewels; their color was exquisite and beautiful. When the Buddha stepped upon them, as well as when the various bodhisattvas stepped upon the flowers, they all produced five hundred petals. As for the disciples who rode upon them, the flowers likewise produced five hundred petals.
When Shenri saw the fire pit and witnessed this miraculous transformation, his heart was struck with alarm and he was seized by great terror; he prostrated himself, bowing his head to the ground.
Once the Buddha had entered the house and the Bodhisattvas and disciples were all seated, Shenri repented and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:

"I have been most reckless and have committed what is contrary to the Dharma. There is poisonous medicine mixed within this meal; I beg you to allow me to prepare another, and to remain for a short while."
The Buddha said, "Bring the poisoned rice; I shall eat it myself.

Shenri rejoiced and immediately followed the Buddha’s instruction. He distributed the food and utensils until they were spread everywhere, and then the Buddha accepted them, reciting verses of blessing and giving a formal dedication of merit (*dakṣiṇā*).

That poisoned rice was transformed into a hundred flavors, its fragrance pervading the ten directions. Any who smelled the aroma of this rice were spontaneously satiated and their bodies attained peace and stability; they all gave rise to the supreme mind of equanimity for the Way.

When the meal was finished, the five hundred ladies and Cāṇḍāla Dharma paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side. The elder Śinju took a small seat for himself and sat before the Buddha, addressing him thus:

"World-Honored One, you possess supernatural powers and the three types of penetrating knowledge. You must have already known my intentions; yet you did not immediately inform me, instead causing us to commit this unrighteous act and create this evil deed. Could it be that the Buddha was unaware of what we were plotting?"
The Buddha told Shenri:

"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha. His radiance was immeasurable as he delivered those who were weary and despondent; accompanied by an infinite multitude of bodhisattvas and great disciples, he entered a city."
At that time, there was an elder named Vidūra who had just come out of the city. There was a daughter of a brahmin, peerless in her fresh and pure beauty, holding famous flowers.
Then the elder’s son gave five hundred silver coins to the flower-seller and obtained five stalks of flowers, which he scattered over the Buddha.
The Buddha then bestowed upon him the prediction, saying:
"After an incalculable number of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.

When you become a Buddha, there will be an elder named Shenri who, in collusion with heretical practitioners, will conspire to commit an act of rebellion, intending to test you with a pit of fire and poisoned rice."
"Though you possess such evil, you shall attain liberation through me.
The Buddha said to Śūṇa:

"The son of the elder at that time was none other than my present self. At that moment, having received the prediction from the Tathāgata, I immediately attained the samādhi of clear discernment; thus, I already fully anticipated your very name, let alone the matters you plotted yesterday—how could I not have known them?"
"You should know that the Buddhas’ wisdom of skillful means intends to give rise to awakening through causes and conditions.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had said, the elder Śiṅgālaka immediately attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) and further exclaimed:
"The Tathāgata’s wisdom is such that there is nothing it does not deliver; he clearly knows that I shall no longer undergo retribution for my sins."

Why is this? In a past life, Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata already prophesied my name, saying that I would now be transformed and enlightened by a Buddha; for this reason, I shall no longer undergo further retribution.

At that time, while the Buddha was preaching the Dharma in Rājagṛha, thousands of countless elders and householders, as well as a multitude of five hundred followers of other paths, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The five hundred ladies immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression.
The youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, praised the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

"If in a future age I should attain Buddhahood, may all the people in my land be free from evil intent and be simple and honest. As for those evil lands where the people are stubborn, and the world is debased by the five turbidities, I vow to transform and enlighten them therein."
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Did you hear what the youth Candraprabha has said? Ānanda replied:
“Yes, I have heard it,” [replied Ānanda]. The Buddha told Ānanda:

“A thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, when the sūtras and the Dharma are on the verge of being extinguished, the youth Candraprabha shall appear in the state of Qin as a sagely ruler, upholding my sūtras and the Dharma to cause the transformation of the Way to flourish.”

The land of Qin and all the frontier kingdoms—Shan-shan, Uḍḍiyāna, Kuci, Kashgar, Bactria, and Yarkand—as well as the various Qiang, Lu, Yi, and Di peoples, shall all revere the Buddha and the Honored Dharma, and universally become bhikṣus.
If there are any men or women who hear this *Śunirjīva Sūtra*, all the evil and rebellious offenses they have previously committed shall be completely eliminated.

One should know that those whom the World-Honored One is to deliver are of such a nature; if even those who have committed rebellious offenses can attain liberation, how much more so for those who study the Buddha-way with a sincere heart!
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the entire assembly was filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.

According to the *Kaiyuan Lu*, among the four translations of this *Śūnyatā-sūtra* (or *Śunyata-sūtra*), one has been lost. Although the translation by Dharmarakṣa contains the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra*, which is also titled the *Śunyata-sūtra*, this is merely one sutra having two names; it is not the case that there is a separate *Śunyata-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa.
Since the *Candragarbha-śrāmaṇera-sūtra* already exists in the Tibetan canon, translated by Dharmarakṣa, that matter is settled!
Why then is there yet another *Śunyatā-sūtra* (or *Śunika-sūtra*) attributed to Dharmarakṣa’s translation?
Thus, it remains unknown by whom this sutra was translated,
and on what basis can it be asserted that it was translated by Dharmarakṣa?
Now, based on the fact that the catalogue states:

"In the translations by Zhi Qian, there is one fascicle of the *Śūnyatā-sūtra* (Shenri jing), which is said to be a different translation of the same original text as the *Candraprabha-kumāra-bodhisattva-sūtra*.
Now, upon examining the phrasing and sentences, the two sūtras do not differ; therefore, they have not been presented together," and so forth.
"There must have been a *Candraprabhakumāra-sūtra*, also known as the *Śūnyatā-sūtra* (or *Shenri jing*), translated by Zhi Qian within that collection.
It is no longer found in any of the current canons; it is likely this very sūtra, and its title has been erroneously attributed to Dharmarakṣa."
Thus, the four translations are now complete once again.
I venture to present these humble words to await the discernment of future sages.
